title: Trade statistics can identify biodiversity-linked products while still missing ecosystem provenance, social sustainability, and who captures value across the chain
source_unit: United Nations Trade and Development, Towards a framework for enhanced trade and biodiversity statistics
geography: 193 economies in the TraBio trade-data scope; biodiversity-based supply chains, rural livelihoods, firms, communities, regulators, and global biodiversity-policy monitoring

observations.period: 2010-2026; biodiversity-linked trade measurement and policy scope

denominator.unit: economies covered by UNCTAD's Trade and Biodiversity statistical tool scope

biodiversity_product_subheadings.unit: distinct biodiversity-based products covered by the TraBio classification, measured through HS subheadings

population_dependence.unit: percent-plus of the world's population estimated to depend on biodiversity for livelihoods

rural_poor_vulnerable_dependence.unit: percent of the world's poor and vulnerable people living in rural areas and depending on biodiversity for livelihoods, approximately

statistical_limit.value: trade statistics do not show whether products are sustainably produced or how trade affects biodiversity and livelihoods

observations.method: UN Trade and Development framework combining trade classifications, biodiversity-linked product data, value-chain concepts, and policy-monitoring needs.
observations.uncertainty: Product classification and trade flows do not establish extraction practices, ecosystem condition, labor conditions, benefit sharing, or causal livelihood effects; population-dependence estimates are broad contextual measures.
observations.subgroup: Rural households, small producers, Indigenous and local communities, biodiversity-based firms, exporters, consumers, regulators, and conservation institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Trade can create incentives for conservation, rural diversification, employment, and resilient livelihoods when social and environmental safeguards and benefit-sharing are credible.

observations.period: 2026; expert framework and supply-chain traceability priorities

denominator.unit: institutions represented in the informal UNCTAD working group on trade and biodiversity statistics, more than

institution_count.unit: institutions represented in the informal working group, more than

value_chain_stages.value: ecosystems, collection, cultivation, production, processing, trade, and where relevant consumption

data_system_priorities.value: standardized definitions, linked databases, data sharing, and stronger capacity in developing countries

future_traceability.value: greater supply-chain transparency and a unified open biodiversity-trade database are proposed as longer-term directions

observations.method: UNCTAD synthesis of expert working-group discussions and proposed statistical architecture for connecting trade records to ecological and production contexts.
observations.uncertainty: A proposed framework is not an operational traceability system, complete database, verified chain of custody, or evidence that participating institutions agree on implementation details.
observations.subgroup: National statistical offices, customs agencies, biodiversity authorities, firms, producers, communities, researchers, and international organizations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Incremental linkage of existing datasets may produce useful monitoring before a unified database exists; traceability can also impose costs and privacy or sovereignty concerns.

denominator.unit: existing indicators preselected for the proposed trade and biodiversity statistical framework

environmental_indicators.unit: preselected indicators relating to environmental sustainability

economic_indicators.unit: preselected indicators relating to economic sustainability and trade

policy_indicators.unit: preselected indicators relating to policy and governance

social_indicators.unit: preselected indicator relating directly to social sustainability

social_measurement_gap.value: decent work and wages, gender equality, land use and rights, food equity, and Indigenous peoples are identified as future data needs

observations.method: UNCTAD prioritisation of existing indicators using criteria including data availability and interoperability, with separate accounting of environmental, economic, policy, and social dimensions.
observations.uncertainty: Indicator counts reflect a proposed selection, not the full universe of possible measures or their quality; one social indicator does not prove that social harms are absent or that environmental metrics are complete.
observations.subgroup: Workers, women, Indigenous peoples, land-dependent communities, food-insecure households, firms, regulators, and conservation and development organizations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Prioritising available and interoperable indicators can make a framework usable now; social dimensions may require new surveys, administrative data, geospatial methods, and locally governed data systems.

biodiversity_services.value: food, medicines, materials, climate regulation, and water filtration

trade_risk_set.value: overexploitation, habitat destruction, and invasive-species spread can accompany trade

biotrade_implementation_scope.unit: countries where UNCTAD BioTrade Principles and Criteria are reported as implemented or fostered, more than

governance_tradeoff.value: trade can support jobs and resilient livelihoods or intensify ecological and distributional pressure depending on production and benefit-sharing rules

observations.method: UNCTAD policy framework linking biodiversity-based trade, ecosystem services, rural livelihoods, conservation, and BioTrade principles.
observations.uncertainty: The framework and implementation count do not establish compliance, ecological recovery, fair benefit distribution, job quality, or household resilience in participating countries.
observations.subgroup: Rural and Indigenous communities, small producers, women and youth, biodiversity-based enterprises, consumers, governments, NGOs, and conservation actors.
observations.counterinterpretation: Local value addition and transparent benefit-sharing can align trade with conservation and livelihoods; restrictions without viable alternatives can shift extraction or worsen rural insecurity.

related_sources.claim: UNCTAD TraBio data hub and biodiversity-based product trade-data context.
UNCTAD BioTrade principles, livelihood, conservation, and policy context.

boundary: This record adds a biodiversity-trade route from product flows through ecosystem provenance, value-chain traceability, rural livelihoods, social sustainability, and governance. It is a statistical-framework publication, not ecological monitoring, respondent data, verified sustainability, household causal evidence, or proof that BioTrade implementation produces equitable outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official UNCTAD trade-biodiversity publication page, BioTrade topic page, and TraBio data-hub context were reviewed; economy and product coverage, population dependence, working-group scope, proposed value-chain stages, indicator composition, social-data gap, ecosystem functions, and BioTrade implementation claims were cross-checked.
